content_units: California Non-Compete Snapshot

For a former software sales employee in California, a broad post-employment non-compete like “no work for a competitor in the US for 12 months” is often a major issue to review closely, especially when there was   no sale of business  . That said, the practical answer is usually not just “is it enforceable,” but also whether the employer might still send demand letters, assert trade secret/confidentiality concerns, or try to frame the dispute around customer relationships, solicitation, or misuse of data.
Context for this situation
- Employment ended:   2026-01-15
- Planned new role:   March 2026
- Restriction:   12 months, competitor-wide, throughout the US
- Stated carve-out:   no sale of business involved
- Likely governing location to examine first:   California
Key Issues to Review With Counsel
Issue   Why it matters   What to check   Likely practical impact

California non-compete rules   California is generally hostile to employee non-competes   Contract governing law, forum clause, where employee lived/worked, where work was performed   May strongly affect leverage and risk analysis

Scope of the restriction   A 12-month nationwide competitor ban is broad   Exact wording of “competitor,” “work for,” and whether it bars all roles or only sales roles   Broader wording can increase intimidation value, even if vulnerable legally

Non-solicit language   Sometimes employers rely more on customer/employee non-solicit terms than the headline non-compete   Separate sections on customers, prospects, employees, partners, and recruiting   Could affect outreach plans after joining new employer

Confidentiality and trade secrets   These claims are often the real litigation focus   NDA, confidentiality clauses, CRM exports, pipeline reports, pricing sheets, customer lists, Slack/email forwarding   Biggest day-to-day risk if any data was retained or used

Return-of-property compliance   Employers look for device/data retention issues   Offboarding certification, laptop return, cloud drives, personal email, phone backups, downloads   Clean return history can reduce dispute risk
Choice-of-law / venue clauses   Contract may point to another state or arbitration   Arbitration clause, forum selection, delegation language, class waiver   Can change cost, speed, and strategy

New job overlap risk   Similar territory/accounts can trigger threats even without a valid non-compete   Same customers, same product segment, same pricing intelligence, same team moves   Practical risk may rise if role looks highly competitive
Likely Practical Implications for a March 2026 Move

A March 2026 start date is still well within the contract’s stated 12-month restricted period, so the clause may matter   practically   even if its legal force is doubtful. The main real-world question is whether the former employer is likely to object and on what theory.
What often matters in practice
-   The former employer may still send a warning letter
- This can happen even where the clause looks overbroad.
- The goal is often deterrence, delay, or pressure on the new employer.
-   The new employer may ask for paperwork
- Offer letters sometimes require disclosure of restrictive covenants.
- They may want written assurance that no confidential information will be brought over.
-   Trade secret allegations can become the central issue
- In software sales, this may focus on:
- customer lists
- renewal timing
- pricing and discount strategy
- pipeline and forecast data
- product roadmap or deal strategy
-   Account overlap can increase risk
- If the March 2026 role covers the same named accounts, region, or buyer set, that can create more friction.
- Risk is often lower if the new role is ring-fenced away from former accounts initially.
-   Conduct after departure matters a lot
- Downloading files before exit, forwarding emails, retaining contacts from internal systems, or soliciting former team members can all complicate the picture.
Risk signals that deserve extra attention
- You signed multiple agreements, not just one offer letter.
- The contract includes   arbitration   or a non-California venue.
- The old employer has sent a cease-and-desist before in similar situations.
- You handled strategic accounts, pricing authority, or sensitive pipeline data.
- You contacted former customers or coworkers immediately after departure.
- The new company is a direct head-to-head competitor in the same segment.
Lawyer Prep Checklist
Option 1: Employment agreements packet   Gather every signed restriction-related document in one folder   Best for fast legal review
Gather contracts
- Offer letter
- Employment agreement
- Confidentiality / NDA agreements
- Non-compete / non-solicit addenda
- Equity award agreements if they contain restrictive covenants
- Commission plans or sales compensation plans
- Arbitration agreement
- Employee handbook acknowledgments
- Separation agreement, if any
- Exit certification / return-of-property confirmation
Option 2: Job-change comparison file   Show exactly how the old and new roles compare   Helps counsel assess practical risk
Compare roles
- Old job title and duties
- New job title and duties
- Old territory / account list / segment
- New territory / account list / segment
- Whether the new role touches the same customers, prospects, or channel partners
- Whether compensation incentives are tied to the same market or accounts
Option 3: Data-handling record   Document what you did and did not keep after exit   Critical for trade secret analysis
Review data
- Whether any files were downloaded before departure
- Whether company data exists on personal devices, drives, or email
- Whether cloud sync tools captured work files
- Whether you retained CRM exports, call notes, pricing sheets, or forecasts
- Whether all devices/accounts were returned or wiped as instructed
Option 4: Timeline and communications log   Build a simple chronology from exit to new offer   Useful if a threat letter arrives
Build timeline
- Notice date
- Last day worked
- Separation date:   2026-01-15
- First contact with new employer
- Offer date and planned start date
- Any contact with former customers/coworkers after departure
- Any messages from former employer about restrictions
Questions to Bring to an Employment Lawyer
- How likely is California law to control this dispute based on where the work was performed and what the contract says?
- Does the clause look like a true non-compete, or are there separate restrictions that matter more?
- Are there any parts of the agreement that might still be argued separately, such as confidentiality, trade secrets, or customer non-solicitation?
- Does the   12-month US-wide competitor ban   create practical risk even if it may be vulnerable under California law?
- Should the new employer be told about the clause, and if so, how should that be framed?
- Would it help to ask the new employer for a   narrowed role  , delayed account access, or a no-solicit firewall for former accounts?
- Are there facts that make an injunction threat more or less likely?
- Does the contract require arbitration or litigation in another state?
- What should be done immediately if a cease-and-desist letter arrives?
- Is it advisable to send any proactive response now, or better to wait?
- What evidence should be preserved to show no misuse of confidential information?
- Are there any risks from personal devices, synced folders, LinkedIn contacts, text messages, or personal email?
- What should the client avoid saying to the new employer, old employer, customers, and former coworkers?
Sensible Next Steps Before the Consultation
- Keep the review focused on   documents, data handling, and account overlap  .
- Do not delete potentially relevant messages or files; preserve them.
- Do not use any former employer documents, lists, or internal notes in the new role.
- If possible, prepare a one-page factual timeline and a side-by-side role comparison.
- If the new job can be structured to avoid former accounts at first, that is often worth discussing.
